newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Sino Land's aggressiveness seen paying off.
newsitem.headline: Sino Land's aggressiveness seen paying off.

text.p: Sino Land Co Ltd's aggressive accumulation of land is likely to pay off, property analysts said on Wednesday, the day after the property developer paid a record price for a plot in a government land auction.
"There are good grounds to believe that Sino (Land) in three years' time will realise a respectable return on its investment," said Adam Osborn, property analyst at BZW Securities.

A consortium owned equally by Sino Land and chairman Robert Ng's family paid a record HK$11.82 billion (US$1.53 billion) for the 25,592 square metre site in Chai Wan on eastern Hong Kong island at Tuesday's auction.
Obsorn said the price exceeded expectations of about HK$9.7 billion, but added he still regarded it as reasonable.

"If they can get the product mix right in the way that Cheung Kong has done it in Laguna Verde then I think by the time we get to 2001 and look back I think actually the price they paid for the land would look reasonable," Osborn said.
Cheung Kong (Holdings) Ltd packaged its Laguna Verde development in the industrial area of Hunghom on the Kowloon peninsula as luxury residences and sold the flats for about HK$9,500 per square foot.
The price paid for the Chai Wan site showed the confidence developers have in the market, said Winnie Chiu, an analyst at DBS Securities.
Sino Land said it would invest HK$20 billion in developing the seafront site into a complex comprising 300,000 square feet shops and two million square feet of residential property.
Sino Land would need to sell the units at HK$9,500 per square foot to get a 15 percent return on its investment, Osborn said.
Analysts put the breakeven price at between HK$7,500 and HK$8,000 per square foot.
Brokers said fears of a possible cash call by the company after the auction dampened interest in its stock, which was down HK$0.40 at HK$8.05 in late trade on Wednesday.
Chiu said there were several fundraising options open to Sino Land.
"What I would worry about is the gearing of the company as they might do loans and MBS (mortgage backed securities)," she said.
Sino Land's current gearing was about 35 percent, Chiu said.
Analysts said Sino Land had gained a reputation for paying top dollar in land auctions at the peak of the market.
"What they have basically done is bought land consistently throughout the cycles. Yes, they caught the top but also more importantly is they caught the bottom of the market," Osborn said.
Sino Land successfully expanded its land bank in 1995 while many of the medium size developers missed the bottom by trying to second guess the market.
The company has bought at least six plots of land at government land auctions since March 1995.
